title: CROSS JOIN
description: A CROSS JOIN pairs every row of one table with every row of another - no ON condition, no matching required, just every possible combination. Write a query that returns every possible pairing of a department's `name` with a distinct product `category` (useful for a budget-planning report template that needs one row per department/category combination, even before any real spending data exists).
hints: 💡 SQL concept to consider: CROSS JOIN
CROSS JOIN has no ON clause because there's nothing to match - if the left side has 5 rows and the right side has 3, the result is all 15 combinations, every left row paired with every right row.
CROSS JOIN departments with a subquery that selects DISTINCT category FROM products, aliasing that subquery as a table so you can name its column.
expected_behavior: Returns one row for every (department, category) combination - department count times distinct category count.
solution: SELECT departments.name, categories.category FROM departments CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT category FROM products) AS categories;
explanation: CROSS JOIN is rare in everyday querying (most joins need an ON condition, or you'd get a combinatorial explosion) but it's exactly right when you deliberately want every combination - like generating a full grid template before any real data fills it in.
postgres_note: Writing two tables separated by a comma in FROM (FROM a, b) is old-style implicit CROSS JOIN syntax - Postgres still accepts it, but explicit CROSS JOIN reads much more clearly.
